title: The New Right’s Grand Strategy After Trump
gist: A Carnegie fellow argues the U.S. New Right is forging a fourth grand-strategy school—'civilizationism'—that would restructure the world into bounded civilizational spheres each run by a hegemon, granting Russia eastern Europe, tolerating Chinese hegemony in Asia, abandoning Israel, and dominating the Western Hemisphere; it diverges sharply from Trump's actual transactional foreign policy but is poised to gain clout after his catastrophic Iran war.

themes.theme: Civilizationism as a new grand-strategy school

insights.claim: The New Right is forging a fourth U.S. grand-strategy contender—'civilizationism'—alongside the established schools of restraint, liberal internationalism, and primacy.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Names an emerging worldview that could redefine U.S. alliances and force posture—a framework for reading post-Trump foreign policy.
insights.quote: the New Right, is forging a new contender: call it “civilizationism.”
insights.locator: The debate about American grand strategy

insights.claim: The New Right defines the West not by shared creedal principles like democracy and equality but by a specific geographic territory, shared ancestry, and Christianity.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: The ethnoreligious redefinition of Western identity is the root from which all the strategy's alliance implications follow.
insights.quote: the West is defined by a specific geographic territory, a shared ancestry, and Christianity
insights.locator: The notion that there is a Western civilization

insights.claim: Civilizationism would structure the world into bounded civilizational spaces each dominated by a hegemon, with the U.S. as hegemon of the West pursuing coexistence with China rather than global leadership.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: A spheres-of-influence world order would upend the post-Cold War security architecture underpinning global markets and alliances.
insights.quote: Civilizationists would aim to structure the world along bounded civilizational spaces, each dominated by a hegemon.
insights.locator: Extended to the realm of foreign policy

insights.claim: Civilizationism's intellectual logic is more Schmittian than Huntingtonian, drawing on Nazi jurist Carl Schmitt's idea of Grossräume—spatial blocs dominated by regional hegemons that coexist because they accept different political systems.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Identifies the doctrine's true intellectual lineage—useful for anticipating that its logic favors coexistence and spheres over civilizational clash.
insights.quote: The New Right’s logic of civilizationism, however, is more Schmittian than Huntingtonian.

themes.theme: The New Right's rise to power

insights.claim: The New Right comprises postliberals, Claremonters, and national conservatives united by rejecting limited government, neoliberal economics, and hawkish foreign policy, and by viewing liberalism as the cancer of Western civilization.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Maps the coalition and its break from traditional conservatism—signals policy volatility on trade, economics, and alliances.
insights.quote: the movement sees liberalism not as the foundation but as the cancer of Western civilization

insights.claim: The New Right is institutionalizing power through the Claremont Institute, a Trumpist Heritage Foundation, and new entrants, with at least 70 Claremont fellowship alumni—including the OMB director and deputy national security adviser—serving in the administration.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Personnel penetration means the ideology has a durable staffing pipeline that outlasts any single election cycle.
insights.quote: at least 70 alumni of Claremont fellowships, including the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget and the deputy national security adviser, serve in the current administration

insights.claim: JD Vance is the movement's figurehead, flanked by Ron DeSantis, Josh Hawley, and Tucker Carlson, with Michael Anton as its leading foreign-policy thinker.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Identifies the individuals whose ascendance would advance civilizationism—names to track in 2028 succession scenarios.
insights.locator: The New Right has now drawn unprecedentedly close

themes.theme: Divergence from Trump's actual foreign policy

insights.claim: Despite civilizational rhetoric, Trump's actual foreign policy diverges from civilizationism because his behavior is driven by personal grievance, transactional impulses, and enriching his kin and clique.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Distinguishes rhetoric from practice—civilizationism is a future contender, not current policy, so don't read Trump's moves as its blueprint.
insights.quote: Trump’s behavior is primarily motivated by personal grievance, transactional impulses, and a private interest in maximizing the wealth of his kin and clique

insights.claim: The biggest rupture between Trump and civilizationism is the Middle East: contrary to campaign promises he launched a regime-change war on Iran and treats Israel as a privileged ally, resembling neoconservative hawks.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: The Iran war is precisely the move civilizationists opposed, seeding the intra-party backlash the author expects to boost them.

insights.claim: The New Right is much less interested in championing Israel, driven by rising conspiratorial anti-Semitism, declining Christian Zionism, a belief the alliance traps the U.S. in costly wars, and revulsion at Israel's Gaza campaign among younger conservatives.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: A generational conservative shift away from Israel signals possible long-run erosion of bipartisan U.S. support—material for Middle East risk.
insights.locator: The American New Right is much less interested

themes.theme: Implications for China, Russia, and Europe

insights.claim: Civilizationism prescribes consistent military withdrawal from East Asia tantamount to tolerating Chinese hegemony, with New Right thinkers calling China a 'civilizational equal' and Michael Anton stating Taiwan is not worth fighting over.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: An explicit willingness to cede Taiwan and Asia would upend East Asian security and supply chains—a tail risk for the region.
insights.quote: Taiwan is not worth fighting over
insights.locator: Civilizationism also prescribes a different approach to China

insights.claim: A civilizational grand strategy would not treat Russia as a threat and would end the U.S. security commitment to Europe, granting Moscow a sphere of influence over eastern Europe.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: De facto abandonment of NATO's eastern guarantee is the sharpest break—directly relevant to European defense and Ukraine outcomes.
insights.quote: A civilizational grand strategy would not treat Russia as a threat and, thus, not sustain the U.S. security commitment to Europe.
insights.locator: A civilizational grand strategy would not treat Russia

insights.claim: Civilizationism casts Europe as both the historic cradle of the West and the source of its greatest threat—liberalism—justifying aggressive interference to back far-right forces and ultimately 'culturally vassalize' Europe.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: U.S. interference in European domestic politics would strain the transatlantic relationship independent of the security question.
insights.locator: Civilizationists see Europe as both the historic cradle

insights.claim: Civilizationism requires U.S. dominance over the Western Hemisphere—by military intervention if necessary—because migration and drug inflows are seen as undermining societal homogeneity.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Frames hemispheric assertiveness and hardline migration policy as strategy, not improvisation—watch for interventionism in Latin America.
insights.locator: Civilizationism has already had a strong influence

insights.claim: Two factors favor the New Right in the intra-party battle: a generational divide with younger Republicans favoring reduced Middle East involvement and less China hawkishness, and the backlash from Trump's catastrophic Iran war, which the movement opposed from the start.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Demographics plus the Iran-war fallout are the catalysts to watch for civilizationism gaining ground toward 2028.
insights.quote: As the consequences of this strategically catastrophic campaign become ever more apparent, the New Right’s clout is set to grow
insights.locator: But at least two factors seem to favor

insights.claim: Civilizationism is riddled with contradictions: civilizations have no fixed ethnic, cultural, or territorial boundaries, so a civilizational order would likely produce overlapping claims and regional wars rather than peace.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Flags that even if adopted the doctrine is unstable—undelineated spheres are a recipe for conflict, not the stability it promises.
insights.quote: It is also unlikely that a civilizational order would be peaceful.

insights.claim: The New Right is not unitary—national conservatives oppose loosening ties with Israel and tolerating Chinese and Russian imperialism, and foreign policy remains an afterthought to the movement's domestic focus.
insights.speaker: Leonard A. Schuette
insights.so_what: Internal division means civilizationism is not a foregone outcome even if the New Right wins power—handicap the probability accordingly.
insights.locator: The New Right is also not a unitary camp
